query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Dynamic passivation kinetics—namely the repeated removal and regrowth of a protective oxide layer—dominates the coupled wear–corrosion response in high-entropy alloys. Under sliding contact in a corrosive medium, mechanical abrasion repeatedly disrupts the nascent passive film, exposing fresh alloy surfaces to accelerated corrosion; total degradation then depends on how rapidly the film can reform and effectively protect the underlying alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A representative high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCrTiZrMo or CoCrFeNi-based) in a homogenized/annealed state, with an initially intact passive film formed in a chosen electrolyte.
generation.intervention: Conduct real-time tribo-electrochemical tests while varying the applied normal load and solution chemistry, combined with in situ characterization (e.g., confocal Raman or synchrotron X-ray) to track film breakdown and regrowth on the sliding interface.
generation.conditions: Wear testing in a corrosive solution, at controlled pH and dissolved oxygen level, with loads and sliding speeds spanning typical tribological contact scales, ensuring that the environment and mechanics together challenge the protective oxide film.
generation.structural_mediator: Continuous disruption/reformation of the protective oxide/passive film under friction and corrosion, governed by the alloy’s ability to regenerate the film at sliding interfaces.
generation.mechanism: More frequent disruption or slower regrowth of the oxide film drives synergy: newly exposed active metal sites corrode faster, while corrosion products can alter frictive contact, causing additional mechanical wear and impeding stable passivation.
generation.predicted_outcome: When the film re-forms rapidly relative to the mechanical disruption, total degradation and its wear/corrosion components are significantly lower than in a baseline alloy with slower passivation kinetics. Conversely, if passive films re-form slowly or are highly susceptible to mechanical disruption, total material loss will exceed simple additive wear-plus-corrosion estimates.
generation.baseline: Comparisons are made against the same high-entropy alloy tested under purely corrosive (no sliding) and purely mechanical (inert environment) conditions, where synergy effects are eliminated or markedly reduced.
generation.boundary: Under mild conditions (low load, low aggressiveness, or extremely fast film formation), synergy is minimal. If passivation is sluggish or the surface is severely damaged (e.g., extreme loads or extremely corrosive media), the film cannot protect effectively, and the synergy effect dominates, leading to high total degradation.
generation.uncertainty: If compositional or microstructural changes alter the film’s formation, stabilities, or mechanical properties in unanticipated ways, passivation kinetics may not be the sole driver of tribo-corrosion synergy, introducing uncertainty under new alloy compositions or extreme testing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform an in situ tribocorrosion test at controlled pH using two variations of the same alloy: one with enhanced passivation kinetics (e.g., via doping or annealing to form a dense protective oxide) versus an untreated control sample. Apply incremental loads and measure friction coefficient, electrochemical rest potential, and mass loss in real time.
measurements: Open-circuit potential and corrosion currents (measuring passivation kinetics).
Coefficient of friction and wear scar depth to evaluate mechanical damage.
Morphological and compositional evolution of surface/oxide film using in situ spectroscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If minimal synergy occurs despite slow or unstable film regrowth conditions—i.e., if total mass loss is accurately predicted by the sum of separate wear and corrosion rates—then the hypothesis that dynamic passivation kinetics controls tribo-corrosion in high-entropy alloys is falsified.

AbstractThe challenge of cavitation erosion (CE) in flow-handling components of marine engineering has promoted the development of advanced materials due to safety incidents and economic costs. High entropy alloys (HEAs), known for high hardness and corrosion resistance, emerge as promising candidates. This paper delved into the CE characteristics of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA when subjected to the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, elucidating the synergistic effect of CE-corrosion. The quantitative analysis revealed that CE-corrosion synergy contributed 48.02% to total CE mass loss, primarily attributed to corrosion-induced CE damage. Meanwhile, electrochemical noise (EN) was utilized to reveal the corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution combined with the morphologies observation and surface roughness. Extended CE time compromised the corrosion resistance of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA and diminished the impact of selective phase corrosion on the surface. Eventually, the CE damage mechanism of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA was revealed based on pertinent experimental findings. To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. decision.trend: Early tribological studies on high-entropy alloys emphasized wear behavior (PMC7311485), showing promising low friction and wear resistance under controlled (often inert) conditions. Subsequent work began to incorporate corrosion factors, as seen in cavitation erosion-corrosion tests (PMC11378927), revealing that synergy could account for nearly half of total material loss, yet the underlying mechanistic interactions remained unclear. More recent efforts introduced strategies (e.g., localized doping) to enhance both wear and corrosion resistance (PMC12565319), demonstrating improvements but not fully resolving the fundamental cause-and-effect relationships that govern tribo-corrosion coupling in high-entropy alloys.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how mechanical damage and corrosion co-evolve at the surface—specifically how repeated removal, regrowth, and chemistry of the passive film drive or mitigate total tribo-corrosion damage in high-entropy alloys.
decision.lever: Conduct in situ tribo-electrochemical tests that simultaneously measure friction, wear loss, and electrochemical responses under varied loads, sliding speeds, and solution chemistries, coupled with real-time surface analytics (e.g., confocal Raman or synchrotron XRD) to track film evolution and local chemistry.
decision.why: Given the evidence that removal and reformation of the passive film may be the rate-controlling mechanism for tribo-corrosion, directly monitoring film breakdown and regrowth under mechanical contact and corrosive conditions is the logical next step. This approach will isolate the role of dynamic passivation in total degradation, predict how altering mechanical or chemical variables changes the balance between wear and corrosion, and unambiguously reveal whether passivation kinetics primarily govern the coupled response. If substantial damage still occurs despite stable film formation, the hypothesis that passive-film dynamics dominate tribo-corrosion would be falsified.
